_comment: Human-authored gold answer for the synthetic Art. 28 GDPR data processing agreement. Clause types follow Art. 28(3) lit. a to h in the regulation's own order, plus Chapter V transfers and governing law. _severity_rationale records why each flag carries its severity, so the calibration can be challenged rather than assumed.

_severity_rationale.subprocessor_authorization: high — Art. 28(3)(d) and Art. 28(2) require the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation. The clause appoints sub-processors at the processor's discretion and has the controller waive its right to object, which removes the authorisation entirely rather than channelling it.
_severity_rationale.deletion_return: high — Art. 28(3)(g) requires deletion or return at the controller's choice at the end of the services. Indefinite retention for the processor's own purposes, including model training, converts the processor into a controller for that processing without a lawful basis.
_severity_rationale.audit_rights: high — Art. 28(3)(h) requires the processor to allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or a mandated auditor. Certification-first audit regimes are ordinary market practice and would be medium; this clause expressly excludes inspections, which removes a mandatory element rather than channelling it.
_severity_rationale.international_transfers: high — Chapter V requires an adequacy decision or an Art. 46 safeguard to be in place before a transfer occurs. Permitting transfers now and addressing the mechanism 'if and when the need arises' inverts that sequence.
_severity_rationale.breach_and_dpia_assistance: medium — Art. 28(3)(f) and Art. 33(2) require notification without undue delay. A fourteen day window is materially worse than the controller's own 72 hour obligation can absorb and should be negotiated, but a reviewer who accepted it with reasons would not be negligent.
